newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujral faces first tests in office.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujral faces first tests in office.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral faced his first shock waves in office on Monday after federal police sought to prosecute the head of his political party in a $280 million corruption case.

Compounding Gujral's worries after a week in office was the possibility former finance minister P. Chidambaram's party would decide to remain out of the government, depriving the ruling United Front coalition of a key partner and economic strategist.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) said on Monday that it had decided to prosecute Laloo Prasad Yadav, president of the Janata Dal party and chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, in an investigation into the use of state animal welfare funds.
The 10 billion rupee ($280 million) "animal fodder" scandal involved the alleged misuse of funds from the welfare scheme.
A CBI spokesman said junior Rural Areas and Employment Minister Chandradeo Prasad Varma was among 56 people who were due to be prosecuted. Varma has said he is innocent.
The federal police agency will request authorisation from Bihar governor A.R. Kidwai to indict Yadav, the spokesman said.
If the governor sanctions the move, the CBI will charge Yadav with violating the Prevention of Corruption Act, which carries a maximum penalty of seven years in jail, CBI officials said.
Normally it would take about a month for the CBI to receive authorisation to indict the accused, CBI officials said. In the past Yadav has repeatedly denied involvement in the scandal.

Both Gujral and his ousted predecessor, former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, belong to the Janata Dal, which is the biggest component of the 15-party United Front coalition with 45 of its 178 deputies in the 545-seat lower house of parliament.
Although Gujral was not implicated in the affair, newspapers said the decision to prosecute Yadav could affect his coalition.

"United Front Thrown Into Turmoil", the Indian Express said in a headline. The Statesman said the CBI decision could "have far-reaching implications in Indian politics, which might even lead to the instability of the week-old Gujral government".
News that the CBI planned to prosecute Yadav rocked the Janata Dal, which had been shaken by a power struggle after Deve Gowda lost a confidence vote in parliament on April 11.

Amar Singh, general secretary of the Samajwadi Party, also in the United Front, told Reuters he would urge Yadav to follow the precedent set by other politicians in corruption cases and to step down as Janata Dal president.
Meanwhile, Gujral's government was awaiting word from Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) on whether the regional party would decide to join the government.
The TMC, another important component of the United Front, announced on April 19 it would not join the government after the alliance passed over its leader, G.K. Moopanar, for Gujral.
On Sunday, the TMC left it up to Moopanar to take a final decision, expected on Monday or Tuesday.

Local TMC leaders in the southern state of Tamil Nadu were largely opposed to joining the government, saying the party had been ill treated by United Front partners and needed to focus on fighting its rival, the state's ruling Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), also a part of the alliance.
Chidambaram was the main economic strategist in Deve Gowda's cabinet and drafted the 1997/98 (April-March) budget. The budget is due to be taken up by parliament in a session starting on Wednesday.
